description: A formula over wired inputs — scalars AND matrices. Arithmetic overloads element-wise with broadcasting, `@` is the matrix product. Write several 'name = expr' lines to compute AND output multiple values from one node. A bounded `loop … end` adds iteration and accumulators; 2D and 3D BOOLEANS subtract, union and intersect.
instructions:
Evaluates through the safe expression engine (the same language as a pobj's `vars` / a declaration's `showWhen`).

TWO MODES:
• Single expression (e.g. `steps*tread`) → one output `val-result`.
• A BLOCK of `name = expr` lines → one `val-<name>` output PER line, evaluated top-to-bottom so a later line can use an earlier name (a `vars` block). One Math Engine node then replaces a whole chain of Math / Conditional / Match — or Matrix / Vector — nodes.
• `Algorithms.` holds whole named algorithms — `Q = Algorithms.Inset(P, 0.3)` offsets an outline with mitred corners instead of you rewriting the miter-vector maths each time. An algorithm is NOT a builtin: it is a body of this same language, so the node shows its maths in a read-only foldable block underneath the formula, and what you read there is exactly what ran. Paste it into your own body whenever you want to take it over and edit it.
• Every built-in has a QUALIFIED NAME that reads as documentation: `Matrix.Transpose(A)`, `Vector.Dot(a, b)`, `Reduce.Sum(M)`, `Compare.Greater(A, B)`, `Shape.Union(A, B)`, `Solid.Prism(ring, 0, h)`. Type two letters and the editor offers the matching functions with their full signature, what each argument means and an example. The BARE names (`T`, `dot`, `sum`, `gt`, `union`, `mprism`) remain valid forever and mean exactly the same thing — the qualified form is an alias, so old and new can sit in one body.
• A line starting with # is a SECTION MARKER: `# Winding test` opens a foldable region that runs until the next marker, so a long body reads as named sections you can fold shut instead of one wall of algebra. Purely presentational — the engine ignores # lines entirely, so adding or removing them cannot change a single output. Fold state travels with a saved flow, so a library workflow can ship folded.
• A name starting with `_` is INTERNAL SCRATCH: it lives in the scope exactly like any other definition — later lines read it, a loop accumulates into it — but it publishes NO `val-` endpoint and never reaches a wire. A ported algorithm runs to a hundred-odd definitions, most of them pairwise N×N work matrices; without this every one would add an output row to the node AND be JSON-stringified on every evaluation, i.e. on every slider drag. Name the steps worth inspecting, `_` the rest — Workflows/Operations/straight_skeleton_with_math.json publishes 28 of its 141.

INPUTS — combinable:
• Every INPUT variable (a free variable not defined by an earlier line) gets its own `valin-<var>` endpoint.
• The static `deps` endpoint merges a whole Parametric Object / Input Properties node's values into scope by name in ONE wire.
An explicit `valin-<var>` wire OVERRIDES deps.

LOOPS: `loop <var> in <count>:` … `end` re-runs the block with <var> bound to 0…count−1. `end` is explicit rather than indentation-significant, so a body survives reformatting, and loops nest. Two things this makes possible:
• an ACCUMULATOR that grows across iterations — seed it before the loop (`A = zeros(0,2)`) then `A = vcat(A, part)` inside. An EMPTY operand is the identity for vcat / hcat, so an iteration that produces nothing leaves the accumulator alone instead of wiping it.
• `row(M, <var>)` as a GATHER by a computed index, which constant indexing could not do.
• a WORK LIST, which is how RECURSION is expressed: keep the items in ONE flat matrix with an id column (`W = hcat(V, zeros(n,1))`), take one per pass (`sv = eq(col(W,2), p)`, `compress` for the item and `compress(W, 1-sv)` for the rest), and write any replacements back with new ids. Ragged sub-lists of different lengths then live in a single accumulator, and a divide-and-conquer recursion becomes a flat loop whose bound follows from the input size. To slice a CYCLIC range out of a ring in order, rotate first — `shift(V, 0 - i)` re-bases the ring on element i, after which the two halves are ordinary `sub(...)` slices; a row MASK cannot do it, because compress returns rows in index order and a range that wraps past 0 comes back scrambled. See Workflows/Operations/convex_decomposition_with_math.json.
• a BEST-SO-FAR (an argmin/argmax over a swept parameter): `B = v < best ? cand : B` then `best = min(best, v)`, in that ORDER — the candidate is compared against the OLD best. Swapped, the test never fires and the sweep returns its first candidate. See Workflows/Operations/bounding_ngon_with_math.json.
• an ARGMIN over a whole i×j TABLE, not just a column: build the index matrix once (`IDX = k * m + T(k)`, k = arange(m)) and read the winner as a LINEAR index, `l = min(where(le(TS, min(TS)), IDX, BIG))`, which floor(l / m) and l − m * floor(l / m) split back into the pair. That is what makes a PAIRWISE search — every reflex vertex against every edge — one broadcast expression: put the i-quantities in columns and the j-quantities in rows with T(...), and the whole table of candidate times, hit points and validity masks builds at once. See Workflows/Operations/straight_skeleton_with_math.json.
• a GATHER by a computed index for EVERY row at once, which `row(M,i)` can only do one row per loop pass: a gather is a permutation and a permutation is a MATRIX, so `eq(idx, T(k)) @ M` returns M's rows reordered by the column `idx` in a single product. That is what turns "read each item's NEIGHBOUR" into one line — and applied to an index column carried through a `sortby`, it is also how you get back to the original order afterwards. With the same pairwise machinery, `min(where(le(D2, tol*tol), T(k), BIG), 'rows')` gives coincident points a canonical id (a poor man's spatial hash) and the same table summed is each point's multiplicity. See Workflows/Operations/mitered_join_with_math.json, which needs all three to walk a graph with no ids in it.
<var> is internal — it never becomes a `valin-` endpoint — while anything the COUNT expression reads IS a real input, so `loop i in rows(S)` takes its bound from the wired list. A name assigned inside a loop publishes its value after the FINAL iteration, or 0 if the loop ran zero times. BOUNDED: 10,000 iterations per loop and 200,000 statement evaluations per body, after which evaluation stops where it is — a mistyped count gives a wrong picture, never a hung tab. An unclosed `loop` closes at the end of the body and a stray `end` is ignored, so a half-typed block still evaluates while you edit.
ACCURACY, with a loop: the single-pass promise below does NOT hold — every element-wise result quantises to 1e-6 and that error accumulates across iterations (Workflows/Operations/voronoi_with_math.json measures 0.12 mm worst case over 7,240 vertices).
NOT BAKEABLE: a parametric object's `vars` block is single-pass, so "Save as Parametric Object" refuses a body containing a loop and tells you, rather than copying the loop's lines as if they ran once.

LANGUAGE: + - * / % ^, @, comparisons, == != (on 'strings' too — `config == 'u-shape'`), && || !, cond ? a : b, PI. Numbers may be written in scientific notation (`1e-9`).

MATRICES ARE VALUES. A wire carries a matrix as JSON text, and anything that parses as a rectangular row-major array is lifted into a real matrix — so `val-points` from Space Geometry / Polygon / Vertices, or any Matrix node's `val-matrix`, wires straight into a variable. An N×2 matrix IS a list of N 2D vectors; there is no separate vector type.
• `+ - * / % ^` are ELEMENT-WISE with numpy broadcasting (each dimension must match or be 1, so N×2 combines with N×1 per-row or with a 1×1 scalar).
• `@` is the matrix product A·B.
• `^` is element-wise POWER, so `A^-1` is the reciprocal of every cell. The matrix inverse is `inv(A)`; prefer `solve(K,F)`, which is better-conditioned.
A matrix used where a number is expected (a comparison, a numeric param) reads its [0][0] cell — the same bridge the nodes' `val-value` output uses.

FUNCTIONS
• algebra — T(A) transpose, inv(A), solve(K,F), kron(A,B), rows(A), cols(A)
• row-wise vectors — shift(M,k) cyclic roll of the ROW ORDER (−1 = next neighbour, +1 = previous), or shift(M,k,'cols') to roll ALONG each row (so a sorted row minus its own shift is that row's gap list), normalize(M), perp(M) / perpcw(M), len(M), dot(a,b), cross(a,b), angle(v) or angle(a,b)
• reductions — sum / mean / prod / min / max, with an optional axis: `sum(M)` folds everything to a plain NUMBER (so it can drive an ordinary numeric param), `sum(M,'rows')` → N×1, `sum(M,'cols')` → 1×C
• constructors (a matrix of a WIRED size — no node can make one) — eye(n), zeros(r[,c]), ones(r[,c]), fill(r,c,v), arange(n) or arange(a,b), diag(v) both ways
• order / selection — the operations that change a list's ORDER and its LENGTH. sort(M[,'rows'|'cols']) sorts the values INSIDE each row / column; sortby(M,key) permutes the ROWS by a key column, so a whole point travels with its key — `sortby(P, angle(P - c))` is the CCW ring of a cloud and `sortby(P,0)` the lexicographic-by-x sweep; compress(M,mask) keeps the rows whose mask cell is non-zero, the one operation whose OUTPUT ROW COUNT is data; where(mask,A,B) is the element-wise ternary
• element-wise comparison — gt lt ge le eq ne, each returning a 0/1 mask of the broadcast shape, which is what compress / where eat. A product of masks is their AND, a sum clamped with min(...,1) their OR. `eq` against an index column is how "skip the entries incident to i" becomes a matrix. The comparison OPERATORS are deliberately NOT overloaded: `<` and `>` still read a matrix's [0][0] cell, because every showWhen gate and every ternary depends on a comparison yielding a scalar boolean.
• slice / concat / reshape — sub(M,r0,c0,nr,nc), row(M,i), col(M,j), hcat(A,B,…), vcat(A,B,…), reshape(M,r,c). hcat / vcat are VARIADIC — they take any number of operands and fold left — so assembling a wide per-instance table is one call: an N×6 axis-segment list for a Tube / Ring row is `hcat(x1,y1,z1,x2,y2,z2)`, not five nested pairs with the operands in the wrong visual order. An EMPTY operand is still the identity, so a loop accumulator is unaffected. Indices are constants unless a loop supplies one; reshape is row-major and its r/c MAY be computed, which makes it an interleave — an M×4 of [a|b] rows reshaped to (2M)×2 alternates a's row and b's row
• BOOLEANS — the operations that REMOVE material, which no amount of construction can express. subtract(A,B), union(A,B), intersect(A,B), xor(A,B) on 2D shapes, each a ring list read EVEN-ODD in the format a 2D Render Polygon row draws: N×2 is one ring, N×3 groups one ring per run of the third column. The result always carries the group column, so an outer plus its holes survives onto a wire — that is how a hole becomes expressible at all, and `subtract(outline, sevenCircles)` is a flute's plan in one call. An empty B is the identity for all but intersect, and even then A comes back DISSOLVED, so `union(A, zeros(0,3))` merges a pile of overlapping pieces into one clean outline. inpoly(P,R) is the companion MASK — which rows of P fall inside R, even-odd — feeding compress / where, and it is how a surface gets TRIMMED without a mesh boolean at all.
• 3D BOOLEANS — msubtract(A,B), munion(A,B), mintersect(A,B) on the `[x,y,z,f]` FACE LIST a Polyhedron row reads, so a result wires straight into one and can be subtracted again. Every input face is triangulated first (a triangle is unconditionally planar and convex, which is what the splitter assumes), and a solid whose winding is globally inverted is detected and flipped. The output has T-junctions where a split had no matching neighbour — geometrically watertight, but not manifold; volumes come out exact.
• SOLID CONSTRUCTORS, because a boolean needs solids and every other mesh in the system is made by a render row, i.e. downstream of the formula. mcyl(seg, r, sides[, rEnd]) is a closed cylinder — or a cone when the end radius differs — along an axis SEGMENT `[x1,y1,z1,x2,y2,z2]`, the same wire format the Tube and Ring rows read, so a drill is aimed with geometry already to hand. mprism(ring, z0, z1) extrudes any 2D outline into a closed solid, whichever way it was wound. mlathe(seg, profile, sides) REVOLVES a closed profile of `[t, r]` rows about the axis.
• USE mlathe, NOT A SUBTRACTION, FOR ANYTHING HOLLOW. `msubtract(cylinder, longer cylinder)` is a poor case for BSP: a thin wall's facets straddle the bore's radial planes instead of sitting behind them, so each is split many times — measured at 3.5× / 3.9× / 4.5× the faces of the equivalent revolve at 32 / 48 / 64 sides. A profile is also the truer description: for a bansuri, `(head,0) → (head,R) → (foot,R) → (foot,rBore) → (cork,rBore) → (cork,0)` IS the outer surface, the foot annulus, the bore and the cork face, in six points a maker would recognise. Then spend the boolean on what only it can do — the holes — and subtract them as ONE cutter (`vcat` the drills, or accumulate them in a loop) rather than one call each: eight chained subtractions measured 116k triangles and 3.8 s where a revolve plus one boolean is 3.2k and 74 ms.
• scalars — min max floor ceil round abs sqrt pow sin cos tan atan2 sign log log2 log10 exp; the logarithms are what invert `^`, so a ratio becomes an interval: 12·log2(f/440) is a frequency in semitones, and equal temperament — hole positions on a flute, fret spacing — is `L / 2^(n/12)` one way and a log the other. `log` is natural and guards x≤0 to 0 rather than −Infinity, so one bad cell cannot poison a broadcast column; `sign` lifting element-wise is what vectorises an ORIENTATION test, and a segment-intersection predicate is four orientation signs compared with each other. There is no acos, but `angle(a,b)` is atan2(cross,dot) in degrees and its absolute value is the same unsigned angle; these LIFT element-wise the moment a matrix is passed, so `sin(arange(0,n) * PI / n)` is a source term that varies as a formula.

EXAMPLE — the whole eleven-node inset chain (see Workflows/inset_using_maths_v2.json):
  E  = shift(P,-1) - P
  n  = perp(normalize(E))
  np = shift(n, 1)
  M  = (n + np) / (1 + dot(n, np))
  Q  = P + inset * M
Wire `val-Q` into Polygon's `valin-points`. Each named line stays a separate output, so the intermediates are still inspectable.

EXAMPLE — scalars, unchanged:
  dir = direction == 'ltr' ? 1 : -1
  run = steps * tread * dir
  n1  = (midSteps>0 && midSteps<steps) ? midSteps : floor(steps/2)

ACCURACY: values stay live between lines and are rounded only when published, so a long chain rounds once — a matrix NODE chain rounds after every node.

LIMITS: no indexing by a computed value OUTSIDE a loop — `row(M,i)` under a `loop i` is the gather; without one, a data-dependent ORDER or LENGTH is still expressible with sortby / compress (see Workflows/Operations/convex_hull_with_math.json, which drops and reorders points with no loop at all). `name` (the field) is just the node's header label.

THREE STAGES, NOT ONE. A Math Engine can DECODE before the formulas and ENCODE after them, which is the whole read-compute-write pipeline in one node. Both sections are blank by default and cost nothing when unused — an object's Math Engine is unchanged.

Decode runs Graph Interpreter on a canvas payload and puts its matrices in scope BY NAME, so the body reads `types` and `spaces` as ordinary free variables and the wires disappear. Encode runs Canvas Encoder over what the body published and adds `val-json`.

Neither hides anything: the decoded matrices are published as `val-` outputs exactly as the standalone node publishes them, so they stay inspectable and any other node can still read them. The standalone Graph Interpreter and Canvas Encoder nodes remain — they run this same code — and are still the right choice when a flow decodes twice, or decodes without computing anything.

parameters.label: Formula(s)
parameters.placeholder: one expression, OR several `name = expr` lines — start a line with # to open a foldable section

parameters.label: canvas JSON in — config, blank = off
parameters.help: Runs Graph Interpreter BEFORE the formulas and puts its matrices in scope by name - a, b, thickness, length, types, spaces, areas, plus nodes, nodeTypes, segNodes and the per-element object parameters - so the body reads them as free variables with no wires. `from` names the scope key holding the payload (default canvasJson); `typeNames` is the code table; `nodeParams` / `segParams` name the parameter keys to lift off each element's attached object (published as nodeVals/nodeHas and segVals/segHas). The matrices are published as val- outputs too, so nothing is hidden.

parameters.label: plan JSON out — config, blank = off
parameters.help: Runs Canvas Encoder AFTER the formulas and publishes val-json. `from` maps each encoder input to the name this body publishes it under — {"a": "AllA", "types": "AllK", …}. `objects`, `pixelsPerMeter`, `libraryPath` and `decimals` are the encoder's own settings.
